title: What training do the EU Good Distribution Practice guidelines require for medicine wholesalers?
description: What the EU GDP Guidelines (2013/C 343/01) require for wholesale distribution staff training, the Responsible Person and brokers, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The EU Guidelines on Good Distribution Practice of medicinal products for human use (2013/C 343/01) require every person involved in wholesale distribution to be trained in GDP and to be competent before starting their tasks. Training must be initial and continuing, role-based, delivered under a written program, include falsified medicines awareness, add specific training for products needing stricter handling, and be recorded with its effectiveness periodically assessed. The Responsible Person must keep their own GDP competence current.
keyTakeaways: The guidelines were published on 5 November 2013 in the Official Journal (C 343/1, 23 November 2013), based on Articles 84 and 85b(3) of Directive 2001/83/EC.

Chapter 2.4 requires competence before tasks start, initial and continuing role-based training under written procedures and a written program, records, and periodic, documented assessment of effectiveness.
Training must cover product identification and avoiding falsified medicines; staff handling hazardous, radioactive, abuse-risk or temperature-sensitive products need specific training.

The Responsible Person must have GDP knowledge and training (a pharmacy degree is desirable), is responsible for implementing and maintaining training programs, and must maintain their own competence through regular training.
Brokers' staff must be trained in EU and national legislation and in falsified medicines issues (Chapter 10.3).
jurisdiction: European Union (EU Member States; the EEA applies the same guidelines)
regulator: European Commission (Guidelines 2013/C 343/01), with wholesale distribution authorizations and GDP inspections by Member State national competent authorities
appliesTo: Holders of a wholesale distribution authorization for medicinal products for human use
Manufacturers that distribute their own products (a manufacturing authorization includes distribution of the products it covers)
The designated Responsible Person (RP) and all personnel involved in wholesale distribution activities
Brokers of medicinal products registered in a Member State

sections.heading: What are the EU GDP guidelines and who must follow them?

blocks.text: The EU GDP guidelines set the quality standard for procuring, holding, supplying and exporting medicines for human use, and every wholesale distributor must comply with them. The [Guidelines of 5 November 2013 on Good Distribution Practice of medicinal products for human use](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:52013XC1123(01)) were published as 2013/C 343/01 and are based on Article 84 and Article 85b(3) of Directive 2001/83/EC. They replaced the version published in March 2013, correcting factual errors in subchapters 5.5 and 6.3.

The introduction notes that Article 80(g) of Directive 2001/83/EC requires distributors to comply with GDP principles and guidelines, and that manufacturers performing distribution of their own products must also comply, because a manufacturing authorization includes authorization to distribute those products. Brokers are subject to certain wholesale provisions and to specific rules in Chapter 10. National competent authorities grant wholesale authorizations and carry out GDP inspections. The 2013 guidelines remain the current EU GDP text as at November 2026.

GDP sits downstream of manufacturing GMP. Personnel rules for manufacturing sites are covered in [EU GMP Chapter 2](/regulations/eu-gmp-chapter-2-personnel-training-requirements); Chapter 2 of the GDP guidelines applies the same idea, that correct distribution "relies upon people", to warehouses, transport and trading.

sections.heading: What does Chapter 2.4 require for staff training?

blocks.text: All personnel involved in wholesale distribution must be trained in GDP and be competent before they start work, with continuing training and evidence that it works. The text of section 2.4 reads:

blocks.title: GDP Guidelines 2013/C 343/01, section 2.4 (extract)
blocks.text: "All personnel involved in wholesale distribution activities should be trained on the requirements of GDP. They should have the appropriate competence and experience prior to commencing their tasks. Personnel should receive initial and continuing training relevant to their role, based on written procedures and in accordance with a written training programme."

items: **Falsified medicines:** training "should include aspects of product identification and avoidance of falsified medicines entering the supply chain."

**Products needing stricter handling:** staff dealing with them should receive specific training. The guidelines give hazardous products, radioactive materials, products presenting special risks of abuse (including narcotic and psychotropic substances) and temperature-sensitive products as examples.
**Records and effectiveness:** "A record of all training should be kept, and the effectiveness of training should be periodically assessed and documented."
**Hygiene (2.5):** procedures on personnel hygiene covering health, hygiene and clothing should be established and observed, relevant to the activities carried out.

blocks.text: The guidelines do not set an annual cycle. Distributors define the interval in their written program and should be able to justify it, for example by linking refresher timing to deviations, temperature excursions or procedure changes. See [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: What qualifications and training must the Responsible Person have?

blocks.text: The Responsible Person must meet national qualification rules, have GDP knowledge and training, and keep that competence current through regular training. Section 2.2 requires the wholesale distributor to designate a Responsible Person who meets the qualifications and conditions of the Member State concerned (Article 79(b) of Directive 2001/83/EC). It adds that "a degree in pharmacy is desirable" and that the RP "should have appropriate competence and experience as well as knowledge of and training in GDP."

The RP should fulfill their responsibilities personally, be continuously contactable, and may delegate duties but not responsibilities. Their written job description should define their decision-making authority. Among the twelve responsibilities listed in section 2.2, item (iii) is "ensuring that initial and continuous training programmes are implemented and maintained", and item (ix) is keeping appropriate records of any delegated duties.

Section 2.4 then makes the RP's own development explicit: "The responsible person should also maintain their competence in GDP through regular training." Because RP qualification requirements are national, multinational distributors need to check each Member State's rules in addition to the guidelines.

sections.heading: Which other GDP chapters contain training duties?

blocks.text: Training duties also appear in the transport, operations and broker chapters, and inspectors often test them alongside Chapter 2.

items: **Cool-pack handling (9.4):** "Staff must be trained on the procedures for assembly of the insulated boxes (seasonal configurations) and on the reuse of cool-packs."
**Receipt and transfer to saleable stock (5.4):** control reports or equivalent proof of release for batches from another Member State should be checked by appropriately trained personnel.
**Returns (6.3):** returned products may go back to saleable stock only after examination and assessment by a sufficiently trained and competent person authorized to do so.
**Self-inspection (8.2):** self-inspections should be conducted impartially by designated competent company personnel.

**Brokers (10.3):** "Any member of personnel involved in the brokering activities should be trained in the applicable EU and national legislation and in the issues concerning falsified medicinal products."

blocks.text: Section 4.2 requires documentation to be retained for the period in national legislation but at least five years. Training records are part of that documentation set, so a five-year minimum is a reasonable baseline unless national law requires longer.

sections.heading: What do GDP inspectors usually check in training records?

blocks.text: Inspectors check that training was completed before the task, that it matches current procedures, and that effectiveness was assessed, not just attendance. A practical readiness check:

items: The organization chart and job descriptions for key positions with deputy arrangements (2.3).
The written training program and the written procedures it is based on, with version history.
Completion dates for each staff member that precede their first relevant task.
Specific training records for every person authorized to handle cold chain, controlled or hazardous products.
The RP's qualification evidence and record of ongoing GDP training.
Documented effectiveness assessments and any retraining that followed deviations or self-inspection findings.
Records retained for at least five years or longer if national law requires (4.2).

blocks.text: For assembling the evidence pack, see [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each GDP section to the distributor's procedures, the roles and product categories they govern, and the assessments that show competence before a task begins. When a procedure or seasonal pack-out configuration changes, the affected roles can be found from those links. See [healthcare and life sciences](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences) for more.

faqs.q: Does EU GDP require annual training?
faqs.a: No fixed interval is set. Section 2.4 requires initial and continuing training under a written program and periodic, documented assessment of effectiveness. Most distributors run at least an annual GDP refresher, but the interval should be defined in the program and justified by risk and by effectiveness findings.

faqs.q: Do transport subcontractors' drivers need GDP training?
faqs.a: The guidelines place the responsibility on the supplying wholesale distributor. Where transport is outsourced, the contract must meet Chapter 7 requirements and transport providers must be made aware of the relevant transport conditions (9.2). In practice distributors require and verify GDP-relevant training through the contract and audits.

faqs.q: Must the Responsible Person be a pharmacist?
faqs.a: Not under the EU guidelines themselves. Section 2.2 says a pharmacy degree is desirable and that the RP must meet the qualifications and conditions set by the Member State concerned. Some Member States set stricter national requirements, so the answer depends on the country of the wholesale authorization.

faqs.q: Do the GDP guidelines cover veterinary medicines?
faqs.a: The 2013 guidelines cover medicinal products for human use. Veterinary medicines have a separate framework under Regulation (EU) 2019/6 and its implementing acts, which should be checked separately for distribution personnel requirements.
